newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. urges Zairean rebels to agree to ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. urges Zairean rebels to agree to ceasefire.

text.p: Growing support for rebels winning territory in eastern Zaire has broken into the open in the capital Kinshasa with troops having to intervene to prevent an anti-government march.
In New York, the U.N. Security Council called on the rebels to agree to a ceasefire deal already accepted by the Zairean government.

The rebels, known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo, have so far rejected international pressure for a ceasefire and instead, confident of military victory, want a transitional government in Zaire and elections.

The Security Council urged the rebels "to declare publicly their acceptance" of a five-point U.N. peace plan devised by special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, "in particular an immediate cessation of hostilities".

With the Tutsi-led rebels advancing in eastern and southern Zaire and meeting little resistance from an indisciplined army, more and more people in the vast Central African country now apparently back guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila.
In Kinshasa's sprawling shanty towns, poverty-stricken residents openly expressed support for Kabila, whose name has dominated the headlines of the local newspapers for months.
Soldiers broke up an attempt by the main opposition alliance to march in Kinshasa on Friday in support of talks with Kabila but party militants vowed to regroup and try again on Saturday.

Soldiers from the feared Civil Guard patrolled flashpoints in the city after dispersing opposition militants trying to gather at the central train station for a march in defiance of a government ban on demonstrations.

Jean Claude Mabale, an activist of the radical Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party, called a small crowd to attention and shouted support for Kabila as about 30 gendarmes stood nearby.
"Hello Kabila. You have taken Tingi Tingi. You are taking Kisangani. We are waiting for you in Kinshasa," he declared.

The rebels are advancing on Kisangani, Zaire's third city and a major strategic target in the five-month-old war. It is the headquarters of a now-stalled army counter-offensive to win back territory in eastern Zaire.

"Kisangani should not be seen as the only place of importance. It is only one of the many towns that we will liberate on the way to Kinshasa and the whole country," Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs minister in the rebel administration, told Reuters in the eastern border town of Goma.
Many among the political class in Kinshasa now apparently fear exclusion from any possible future deal with the rebels whose advance looks more and more unstoppable.

Opposition parties -- some had previously sympathised with the government line that Kabila was a puppet of expansionist neighbouring Tutsi-led countries -- have begun jumping awkwardly on to the rebel bandwagon.

"We said that we did not know Kabila the leader of the Tutsis. Now there has been an evolution and we recognise Kabila the Zairean. He is coming back home," said Sumaru Yamba Yamba, national secretary of the nationalist MNCL party.
The rebels took up arms in October, accusing the government of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda all deny government charges they are giving direct military support to the rebels.
Kabila has said there can be no ceasefire until President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is ailing in France and has rejected any direct talks with the rebels, agrees to negotiate an end to his 31-year rule.
